paper_title: Divide and Check: Logical Relations, No Algorithms Attached
statement: Adding exceptions makes the theory immediately inconsistent since ⊥ is inhabited by raise ⊥. Using syntactic models, Pédrot and Tabareau [37] show that the theory enjoys a weaker consistency property: the translation of a closed inhabitant of ⊥ is convertible to the translation of raise ⊥. However, as the authors of [38, p.21] state: “[...]we do not know if canonocity holds for the standard conversion [...] because this result amounts to showing the completeness of computational laws with respect to the new constants introduced”[sic]. The following section answers this question in the affirmative.
context: 4.1 A Primer on Exceptional Type Theory ExcTT presented in Figure 2 extends MLTT with a single operation raise A parametrized by a type A. The term raiseA is an element of A standing for a (call-by-name) exception at that type. When an exception occurs on the left-hand side of an application, it is propagated at the adequate type, the codomain of the application substituted with the argument. Inductive eliminators (indN , ind⊥ ) are adapted to catch exceptions by adding an extra premise (shaded in green ) for the exceptional case, together with a corresponding reduction rule. Adding exceptions makes the theory immediately inconsistent since ⊥ is inhabited by raise ⊥. Using syntactic models, Pédrot and Tabareau [37] show that the theory enjoys a weaker consistency property: the translation of a closed inhabitant of ⊥ is convertible to the translation of raise ⊥. However, as the authors of [38, p.21] state: “[...]we do not know if canonocity holds for the standard conversion [...] because this result amounts to showing the completeness of computational laws with respect to the new constants introduced”[sic]. The following section answers this question in the affirmative. 4.2 Challenges of the Formalization of ExcTT Extending the syntactic metatheory of MLTT to ExcTT presents few challenges, except for the propagation of the typing annotation C of raise C along the reduction rules presented in Figure 2. In these rules, the annotation on the left-hand side is never inspected; instead, the information contained in the annotations of applications or in the arguments of the eliminators is used to determine the right-hand side. As a consequence, there is no need for a congruence rule on exception annotations with respect to ⇝. This implies that raise C is a whnf that is not stuck on a variable, and in particular, is never neutral. The definition of the logical relation must be adapted for type formers whose inhabitants are characterized inductively, namely N, ⊥, U, and neutral types. By contrast, the logical relation for type formers characterized by their elimination rules, such as Π-types, remains unchanged.
